items.title: McNeal Breaux Interview, 1958-11-24
items.q: I recall one time... that Earl Hines came down and he and Boynell got titled down a piano contest

ctx.x: Could he play? His bass is alive. He's a boogie-woogie. Yeah, he played a lot of piano. I mean, he was... I'd say just naturally gifted because he couldn't read. But he could... He could improvise so well. And then... Then Barnell had such a keen ear. He could work in anybody's band. And I don't care what kind of modulation you make, he'll change key along with you. Just the same as if he was reading. As a matter of fact, I recall one time, I think it was on the Pelican, when the Pelican was open, that Earl Hines…

items.title: McNeal Breaux Interview, 1958-11-24
items.q: The interviewee discusses 'Barrel House' (referred to as 'he' and 'Boynell' in the context of the interviewer's question) as a pianist he is aware of and describes his style, but does not explicitly state they played together or had a direct personal interaction beyond general knowledge.

ctx.x: Could he play? His bass is alive. He's a boogie-woogie. Yeah, he played a lot of piano. I mean, he was... I'd say just naturally gifted because he couldn't read. But he could... He could improvise so well. And then... Then Barnell had such a keen ear. He could work in anybody's band. And I don't care what kind of modulation you make, he'll change key along with you. Just the same as if he was reading. As a matter of fact, I recall one time, I think it was on the Pelican, when the Pelican was open, that Earl Hines…
Would you call him Barrel House, Tonk style, or would you say that he played like anybody in particular, or what?

Well, he had... He was another individualist. He had a style of his own. He was more or less on a boogie-woogie style. But he also played some nice blues. And occasionally, he played a pretty nice ballad. But he was really a boogie-woogie piano player. I'd call him that. He was a boogie-woogie man.
